content: The World Health Organization (WHO) Steering Group played a pivotal role in overseeing the development of the guidelines. This group included representatives from WHO headquarters in Geneva, six regional offices, and two country offices. Key contributors included Alarcos Cieza, focusing on disability and rehabilitation at WHO headquarters; Ameel Mohammad, addressing disability, injury, and assistive technology in the South-East Asia Regional Office; and Antony Duttine, specializing in disability and rehabilitation in the Americas Regional Office. Other notable members included Bianca Hemmingsen, working on noncommunicable diseases at WHO headquarters, and Edith Andrews Annan, focusing on medicines and health products in the African Regional Office. The Guidelines Development Group (GDG) provided critical input into the scope of the guidelines, developed key questions in the PICO format, selected and rated outcomes for evidence reviews, and contributed to content development. This group represented diverse expertise across age, gender, settings, and experiences in accessing wheelchair services, health service delivery, and policy development. Members included Alma Kuambu from Papua New Guinea, who brought lived experience and expertise in wheelchair service provision, and Apinchapat Kongkerd from Thailand, a wheelchair service provider, manager, and trainer. Members included Alex Manaila from Romania, a wheelchair service provider, and Ama Adama from Togo, a trainer and service provider. This team included experts such as Steve Milanese and Janine Dizon from the International Centre for Allied Health Evidence in Australia. External partners and observers, including non-governmental organizations and professional associations, participated in the development process. These included representatives from the International Society of Wheelchair Professionals, UNICEF, and the World Federation of Occupational Therapists. To manage conflicts of interest, all contributors completed WHO’s Declaration of Interests (DOI) forms, which were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat. While some individuals declared interests related to their professional roles, such as employment in wheelchair-related organizations or research funding, none were deemed to represent conflicts that would preclude participation. For example, David Constantine held an office representing interests related to the guidelines, and Emma Smith received research funding in related areas. Similarly, Jon Pearlman was involved in wheelchair research and held patents through his employer. Overall, the guidelines were developed through a collaborative and transparent process, ensuring diverse expertise and perspectives while adhering to WHO’s ethical standards.
